items.text:
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Tirana, Albania, has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing cities. This growth has sparked a real estate boom, but locals worry about losing green areas and public spaces. Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) has addressed these issues with its proposal for an upcoming development on Rinia Park, in the heart of Tirana.
Named Fountain Plaza Tirana, the project won over designs presented by four other international firms. Conceived as a mixed-use building, Fountain Plaza Tirana will stand several feet above Rinia Park, preserving and expanding the public park area while making room for a new hotel, apartments, offices, and cultural spaces.
The building evokes a dense cloud formation above the park. To achieve this, layers of rounded, perforated white terraces rest on slim columns, while two wider structures at opposite ends of the building house the elevators that provide floor access. To avoid breaking with the “floating” concept, these elements are clad in flute glass to let light shine through and onto the park.
“We have reimagined urban living in three dimensions—not as a vertical extrusion or a tower competing for attention on the skyline, but as a cloud of homes hovering above the park,” said BIG founder Bjarke Ingels told Dezeen . “Rather than diminishing the park or displacing public life, the building enhances and accommodates both.”
As such, Fountain Plaza Tirana will also feature an open-access library, a covered public auditorium, and community facilities. In addition to the design that lets pedestrians move freely across the park, this aims to make the building’s ground floor a bustling gathering place for city dwellers and visitors alike.
The design also accounts for Tirana’s weather, particularly its hot summers. The structures bring shade to a public park without completely blocking sunlight. Meanwhile, the water features, described as an “inverted fountain,” can cool the area with the effect of a light drizzle. The water used comes from a closed-loop system. With this, the water collected from the building and the green areas at the bottom is stored, filtered, and returned to the park below.

The Other Art Fair , an event devoted to spotlighting cutting-edge creatives, has arrived in Phoenix for the first time. Presented by Saatchi Art, this fair has separated itself from regular art fairs, prompting burgeoning collectors to buy art directly from the creatives themselves, rather than through traditional commercial galleries. The result is a laid-back atmosphere with more accessible prices, all surrounded by live DJs, interactive installations, and family fun.
In its debut year, The Other Art Fair Phoenix brings together 65 local and international emerging and mid-career artists, a curated selection from a pool of 300 applicants. One third of the chosen creatives are Arizona locals, while the rest come from five countries and 14 different states. In addition to this, over half of the artists identify as women.
“We are so excited to bring The Other Art Fair to Phoenix for the first time,” says Nicole Garton, global fair director at The Other Art Fair. “With more than a third of the exhibitor lineup hailing from the State of Arizona, we’re celebrating local talent alongside an international cohort of emerging artists, offering a place for the city’s growing community of art lovers to meet 65 artists all under one roof and come away inspired. Each artist at the fair presents their own artwork, so visitors can ask artists about their practice and methods—and come away with a story and beautiful new artwork for their homes.”
The Other Art Fair experience is based on three simple concepts: meet the artists, learn about their work, and buy it on the spot. It doesn’t matter if it’s your first time buying art or you’re an experienced collector; it’s all about the humans on both sides of the interaction, no middlemen needed. The artworks on sale are even sized so buyers can take them home the same day they purchase them.
Even if you’re just checking out the art, The Other Art Fair offers immersive experiences that add to its more relaxed environment. In The Other Art Fair Phoenix, guests enter the venue through a “garden” of cactus sculptures by artist Will Beger. Civil rights lawyers filed a lawsuit in June and a three-judge panel of the District Court ruled 2-1 that “the enforced segregation of black and white passengers on motor buses operating in the City of Montgomery violates the Constitution and laws of the United States” because the conditions deprived people of equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment.
Alabama and the city appealed, but the decision was summarily affirmed by the Supreme Court, which ordered them to desegregate its buses with an official written notice by federal marshals.
86 years ago today, the animated film Fantasia , conceived and produced by Walt Disney himself, was released. It was only Disney’s third animated film and, though it featured Mickey Mouse in the role of ‘The Sorcerer’s Apprentice’, it had almost no dialogue and consisted of eight pieces of classical music conducted by Leopold Stokowski, including The Nutcracker Suite and Pastoral Symphony .
The 2-hour movie was unable to make a profit that decade, but it was destined to become a classic—and also the 24th-highest-grossing film of all time in the US (adjusted for inflation).
Up until Fantasia’s release, movie soundtracks, LPs, and recordings of all types were presented in mono. Thanks to Disney and Leopold Stokowski’s experimental spirit, the engineering prowess of Bell Labs and RCA—at great cost to Disney— Fantasia brought stereo sound to the masses via a multi-channel system that produced an aural marvel for audiences inside 13 theaters across the country. items.title: What could El Niño mean for winter weather in the US and Canada?
items.desc: El Niño winters typically bring more rain in the southern USA and drier, warmer conditions further north but the impacts on snowfall are complex.
items.text:
Montreal, Canada was badly hit by the Great Ice Storm of 1998 which was blamed, in part, on El Niño.
The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.
This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.
UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact
The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.
This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.
The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.
The latest three month forecast , external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.
South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.
The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.
Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.
California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely.
Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency , external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.
Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.
Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.

School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.
The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues."
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."
The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester.
The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.
The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.
The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts.
Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.
"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.

items.text:
Artist Sally J. Han is an exacting painter with a meticulous eye. Her detailed, colorful works depict some of life’s most ordinary moments—scrolling on a phone, peeling fruit—yet are juxtaposed with surrealist elements. Han often does this through scale. In Satellite of Love , for instance, a diminutive figure wearing a hanbok sits on a rock gazing up at an impossibly large moon that takes over the composition. It’s something we’d imagine many of us doing; however, in Han’s hands, it takes on a fantastical feel that invites many interpretations.
Han has a multicultural background, and art has served as a bridge between cultures. “From an early age, I thought of drawing as a form of communication,” she tells My Modern Met. “Having grown up in South Korea and China, and later moving to the U.S., I sometimes relied on simple sketches to express myself when I wasn’t yet familiar with the language of each country. I had always enjoyed drawing as a child, but living in different countries made it feel less like a talent and more like my own familiar way of expressing myself.”
We follow the same figure throughout Han’s work. Like the artist, the figure exists in different landscapes, including a desert sunset, a verdant tropical garden, and on a large porch with a yard. Carefully rendered elements dot the composition, like animals, tipped-over soda cans, and a pair of eyeglasses held loosely in a hand. Individually, the common objects aren’t anything special. But in Han’s visual language, they become layered and lyrical, touching on ideas of tradition and our own mythology, and ultimately shaped by our own analysis.
“I find that the familiarity and comfort of everyday life can often feel surprisingly new when viewed from a different perspective,” she explains. “I think what I enjoy most is discovering those moments.” Cultures different from her own have always fascinated her. “But what I find even more interesting is the sense of connection we can share despite our differences. I’ve always been drawn to the human side of things, and I think that naturally finds its way into my paintings.”
Han recently concluded a solo exhibition titled Gazing at Lee Art Consulting in Seoul. She’s currently working on paintings that will debut in spring 2027 at Dan Yoshii in New York City.

items.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
items.desc: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
items.text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.
On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope , including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.
"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell , ESA's director of science, said in a statement . Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These " Einstein rings " ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein , who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.
In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

46 years ago today, NASA’s Voyager 1 probe arrived at Saturn and beamed back the first images ever taken of its rings. It arrived at our solar system’s second-largest planet via a gravitational assist trajectory at Jupiter which was replicated with Voyager 2. On November 12th, when the space probe came within 77,000 miles of Saturn’s cloud-tops, the space probe’s cameras detected complex structures in the rings of Saturn, and its remote sensing instruments studied the atmospheres of Saturn and its giant moon Titan. READ what it discovered… (1980)
Voyager 1 found that about 7% of the volume of Saturn’s upper atmosphere is helium (compared with 11% of Jupiter’s atmosphere), while almost all the rest is hydrogen. Since Saturn’s internal helium abundance was expected to be the same as Jupiter’s and the Sun’s, the lower abundance of helium in the upper atmosphere may imply that the heavier helium may be slowly sinking through Saturn’s hydrogen; that might explain the excess heat that Saturn radiates over energy it receives from the Sun.
Winds blow at high speeds on Saturn. Near the equator, the Voyagers measured winds about 500 m/s (1,100 mph). The wind blows mostly in an easterly direction. Voyager measured the rotation of Saturn (the length of a day) at 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds, and identified polar aurorae, and aurora-like ultraviolet emissions at middle latitudes. These remain a puzzle to this day, since bombardment by electrons and ions, known to cause auroras on Earth, occurs only at the high latitudes.

After 100 years, Gretchen Sollo had a major first: a surprise birthday party, thrown by the Lowe’s employees she sees every day.
Following a stroke, Sollo turned to the aisles of Lowe’s for her daily walk and to keep out of the weather in Bradley, Illinois. She’s since walked an estimated 1,500 miles over five years, creating a daily ritual and friendships with staff members that stretched around the store.
Store associates check on her number of laps and even challenge her to races, joining her on her walks around the store. If there’s ever a day Sollo doesn’t show up, staff members notice and worry.
Store manager Joe Jackson gave her the honorary title of “store mom.”
Once Jackson and staff found out Sollo was turning 100 on November 1, 2026, they knew they had to do something special.
When Sollo showed up for her daily laps on October 30, she was joined by Jackson. Jackson guided Sollo over to a decorated aisle where a blue carpet led to an arch of birthday balloons, a cake and a personalized Lowe’s vest for Sollo. The aisle was lined by around 50 associates (some who came on their day off), friends, family and Sollo’s son Hugh.
“I never wanted a birthday party,” Sollo told People in an exclusive interview, adding “Means I missed out on a lot, I guess.”
A woman who spent a century working, raising a family, and staying active finally took a moment to allow others to show how much they cared – they just had to meet her where she already was.

A woman has had her faith in humanity restored after neighbors arrived on paddleboards to rescue her and her son during recent flooding in Florida.
Emergency services were unable to reach her, the 911 operator said, as Brittany Grant and her son sat on their kitchen counter while floodwaters rose higher and higher above their floor.
Brevard County was recently hit by what weather reports say is a 1,000 year rain event, which flooded towns like Melbourne, Port Lucie, and Palm Bay where Grant lives with her son and 3 dogs.
Having had no luck with 911, Grant turned to Facebook asking for help. Seeing the social media SOS, neighbor Stephanie Fanguy marshalled her strapping teenage sons Jonah, 15, and Lucas, 17, who immediately planned a navigational rescue.
Embarking on an inflatable paddleboard and a borrowed kayak, Jonah and Lucas reached Grant’s house and got to work getting her son Nikoa out through what appeared on social media to be the kitchen window.
Lucas tried to calm Nikoa, who told Click Orlando he struggles with anxiety, by asking him simple questions and remarking humorously at the weather.
Eventually, mother, son, and their 3 dogs—including one which took up half the paddleboard—were all brought to safety.
“The community came together and saved us,” she said . “If it wasn’t for them, I don’t know how we would have gotten out.”
“My faith in humanity has been restored,” she added, saying that other neighbors had volunteered to help as well.
Lucas and Jonah, meanwhile, had a hero’s mentality: someone needed help and they didn’t think twice.
“Because they needed help and they were in trouble and danger, so just didn’t think about it and just went to help them,” Jonah said.

items.desc: Every relationship has its fair share of hilarious moments, and many happen during unexpected mishaps. These are the stories you can retell long after they happen, like the images you’re about to see. These are some of the funniest fumbles of wives and girlfriends as they do their best to please their partners.
items.text:
People often say laughter is the best medicine. In romantic relationships, constructive humor can also help calm couples during conflicts.
Licensed psychologist and therapist Jill Harkaway knows this well, having experienced laughter's power in tense moments. She explored this in an article on the Psychotherapy Networker.
As Harkaway points out, humor's greatest power is its ability to regulate emotions. She also notes that it can be hard to stay emotionally reactive while we’re laughing.
“Humor doesn’t change our reality, but it can alter our perceptions of and reactions to it. When partners get stuck in repetitive negative patterns, humor can disrupt the sequence, becoming a metacommunication that can give distance and perspective,” Harkaway wrote .
However, Harkaway also offered a caveat about incorporating humor in relationships. She noted the importance of knowing a partner’s attachment style and the type of humor to use.
People with anxious attachment styles, for example, may respond better to self-deprecating humor, while people with an avoidant attachment style may use aggressive humor to deflect and create distance.
But when it comes to making mistakes as these women did, experts also noted the importance of laughing at yourself. According to Cornell University professor Ovul Sezer , people tend to overestimate how harshly others judge their mistakes, making it hard to take things in stride.
“For minor, harmless blunders, laughing at yourself can signal social confidence, reduce tension, and communicate that the mistake was accidental,” Sezer said .

Nobody ever gets through life without making a few questionable decisions that lead to blunders. And unless they hurt anybody, these comical misadventures often become moments to laugh about later.
Having a partner to witness and even document them makes this shared experience even more memorable, and these women would likely agree. But what about you, dear reader? Which of these made you laugh the most?

items.text:
Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say
An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.
Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.
The new approach, which combines BMI with other body measurements and organ function tests, suggests BMI alone misses obesity in 5-9% of adults, while wrongly diagnosing the condition in as many as 3%.
“This misclassification can account for tens of millions of people, so the inaccuracy of BMI is a big problem at scale and also for individuals,” said Francisco Rubino, a professor of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London.
BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. About 1.6 billion people worldwide are classified as overweight, meaning their BMI falls between 25 and 29.9, and nearly a billion with a BMI of 30 or more are considered obese. Two-thirds of adults in the UK and more than 70% of adults in the US are overweight or obese based on BMI alone.
Rubino and his colleagues drew on health records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain to test a diagnostic approach for obesity that he and other world experts proposed last year in a Lancet Commission report . They used the records to track people’s health for up to 15 years.
Under the new definition, someone with a BMI over 40 is considered obese, but doctors check people with a lower BMI for excess body fat by looking at their waist measurement.
A BMI of 30-plus with a raised waist measurement or waist-to-height ratio counts as obese, as does a BMI from 25 to 29.9 if waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio are high. In most countries, a raised waist measurement means more than 102cm (40in) for men and 88cm for women, while thresholds for a high waist-to-height ratio are about 0.57.
In a second step of the diagnosis, doctors distinguish between clinical obesity, meaning an active disease where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, and pre-clinical obesity, where the extra fat is a health risk but has yet to cause problems.

From the brink of extinction to roaming across 6,500 square miles, populations of Cantabrian brown bears have doubled in Spain over the last 20 years to 370.
Numbering as few as 140 by estimates in the early 21st century, they’re another example of Spain’s ongoing success in protecting several of the country’s endemic species.
Taking its name from the far northern Spanish region whose mountains stand as the bear’s last redoubt, Cantabrian brown bears can actually be found across the regions of Asturians, Leon, Galicia, and Palencia, in addition to Cantabria.
By restricting the movement of animals, the Iberian Peninsula’s northern mountain ranges have led to high rates of endemism in Spain and Portugal among animals such as the wolf, lynx, and bear.
Direct human persecution and the conversion of wilderness to agricultural land gradually impacted the brown bear’s numbers until they could only be found in Cantabria. Yet they clung to existence in the mountains until sufficient protections were put in place for them to gain a second wind.
A study published in 2023 bears witness to the successful survival and spread by Spain’s bears. Published in the journal Conservation Science and Practice, it found that the government’s continual protection measures and establishment of new protected areas, coupled with rural depopulation, allowed the bears to substantially recover.
Using all data available to them, the authors measured the changes in population numbers across 3 periods: from 1982 to 1992, from 1993 to 2002, and from 2003 to 2012.
While a 25% reduction in the numbers of bears was observed between the first 2 periods, this was followed by a 70% increase by the end of the 3rd period. That final period also saw their breeding ranges expand by 30%, such that Cantabria’s 2 breeding populations now overlap, having been separated for decades by an 18-24 mile series of gorges with a highway running through them.
The first 2 periods coincided with the creation of Somiedo Natural Park and Redes National Park respectively, which increased the amount of protected areas centered on the last remaining populations of brown bears 688 square kilometers. Fines for unauthorized killing of bears reached some $350,000.
Additional growth in the geographical range of 77% was observed by the authors between 2013 and 2022 in exactly the proportion and areas they predicted.

On Sunday, November 8, hundreds of people gathered around Chicago’s iconic Cloud Gate sculpture (aka “The Bean”) with one unusual goal: moving it 7 inches to the left. It was quite an ambitious feat, considering the sculpture weighs about 110 tons. Although the crowd was ultimately unsuccessful, the humorous stunt brought Chicagoans together for an afternoon of fun.
The event began with flyers posted around Chicago that simply read, “We need to move the bean seven inches to the left,” with no further explanation. The flyers instructed people to gather at Millennium Park at exactly 12:47 p.m., and the unusual request quickly gained attention on social media.
The reason behind the stunt was an ongoing internet joke that claims a man is trapped inside the sculpture. According to an online invitation for the event, moving The Bean would supposedly reveal a hidden door, allowing people to give the imaginary man a pickle and other resources.
On the day of the event, hundreds of people showed up to participate, with videos showing crowds pushing against the sculpture in unison. Despite their combined efforts, The Bean didn’t budge.
Created by artist Anish Kapoor between 2004 and 2006, The Bean’s nickname comes from the sculpture’s unusual shape. Its 168 stainless steel plates are welded together and polished to create a seamless, mirror-like surface perfect for pictures and selfies. Over the years, it has become one of Chicago’s most recognizable landmarks.
Although the crowd couldn’t accomplish its original goal, the Millennium Park Foundation welcomed the playful gathering. Kathryn Deery, an executive director for the foundation, told People that the event was a creative way to bring people together and celebrate one of the city’s most famous landmarks.
The sculpture remained in place and received its usual cleaning afterward, leaving behind little more than extra handprints and a memorable afternoon for the people who participated.

Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.
The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."
Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not safely landed on Mars
Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.
Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.
His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.
The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.
Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.

items.text:
The National Trust hopes to create new wildlife habitats to attract wildlife including water vole and turtle doves
A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years.
The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey.
The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.
Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate."
The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows.
Northfield is a rich natural site with a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge
Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the tenants.
The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.
Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".
Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.

items.text:
A penned draft of the famous ‘I have a Dream’ speech, written by Martin Luther King Jr. the morning of the famous event on the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after 6 decades.
Unlike any other examples of his longhand writing ever found, the draft’s copious revisions tell of a man who understood the gravity of what he was preparing to say.
The New York Times reports that King’s own draft of the speech had been presumed lost. Those which are known had all been drafted and or typed up by his aides.
Now, Xernona Clayton, the widow of King’s former aide Edward Clayton, has revealed to the nation in its 250th year that she had found the handwritten draft in her deceased husband’s desk drawer in the 1990s, but only recently decided to put it up for auction at Christie’s for the benefit of several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta.
She found it one day in an envelope marked “Speech,” and though she recognized the words immediately, it never occurred to her that it might have been written by the speaker himself.
“This is the most important manuscript I’ve ever had the honor to handle,” Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscript specialist, told the Times, adding that he couldn’t imagine getting his hands on anything better that he “wouldn’t have to steal out of the National Archives.”
This relic of American oratory consists of 7 yellow pages covered in blue ink. Words, and sometimes whole paragraphs are crossed out. In some cases, a word was crossed out to be replaced by another word which was also crossed out.
It captures the mood in the Washington hotel where Dr. King was working on the speech with his colleagues who had spent days exploring various themes and directions it might take. He had been told to limit the speech to 5 minutes—pressure—all while knowing that President John Kennedy had only 2 months prior sent the proposed Civil Rights Act to Congress where it had not yet been voted on—more pressure.

Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread
A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, ⁠a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread.
For decades, ​efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumors, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.
“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in ⁠Newport Beach, California, said in a statement.
Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma.
The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.
When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women ⁠and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women.
In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported.
“For women at high risk, this ​could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Dr Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.
Many such women ‌face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes ‌and ovaries.
“Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”

Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.

"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

An 81-year-old Englishman grew up wondering who his real father was. What he didn’t know was that an entire family tree in Canada was wondering who and where he was.
After being divided by a world war, an ocean, and 8 decades, Rodney Anderson has finally found his long lost relatives with the help of a simple DNA test, and a persistent, curious niece.
“I thought ‘This is a wind up.’ It has to be,” Anderson said, sharing with CBC News the moment he learned of his true origins.
“But it wasn’t. You can’t believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge.”
Anderson’s mother had a child with a visiting Canadian soldier during the Second World War, a secret that his mother and grandmother never shared with him.
He grew up with no knowledge or explanation of his father’s origins whatsoever because of the stigma attached at the time to these out-of-wedlock births, even though they came about during a period of immense crisis and uncertainty about the future.
Canadian Bethany Allen began searching in 2008 for this mystery uncle of hers after discovering in divorce papers that her grandfather, Charles Blakney, had had a child with a woman in the UK in 1944.
He had first sailed off to war in 1942, leaving behind a wife and daughter in New Brunswick. Blakney served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers and returned home in 1945, the same year that Rodney Anderson was born in Farnham to his mother Yvonne. Rumors of his affair overseas remained in the family long after the guns fell silent in Europe.
“My mother [Rodney’s half-sister] had always wanted to know that [Anderson] had a good life and was happy,” Bethany Allen told CBC News.
It took a long time to confirm the link between the Blakney family in Canada and Anderson in Surrey. It came about through a commercial DNA test from Ancestry.

items.text:
The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has finally opened, after 17 years of work put into its creation by George Lucas and his wife, businesswoman Mellody Hobson. While it has drawn large crowds from all walks of life, its proud founders have not forgotten that for many, particularly students and low-income families, museum pricing can be high, resulting in some missing out on a lunch or a treat during a visit. As such, they’ve implemented a few measures to keep it budget-friendly for everyone.
The inspiration behind this lies in Hobson’s personal story. While today she is president and co-CEO of Ariel Investments, and a former chair of both DreamWorks and Starbucks, Hobson grew up in poverty. Her mother, a single parent of six, struggled to make ends meet, sometimes not even having enough money to pay the rent. As a result of this financial challenge, Hobson often found herself unable to afford any food as a kid on a field trip at a museum. These experiences marked her profoundly. In fact, it prompted the couple to create affordable options for all visitors to their museum, where the lobby café offers $2 grilled cheese sandwiches. These simply yet satisfying sandwiches are made with American and cheddar cheese melted together between slices of buttered Pullman bread.
“That was the directive from the founders, George and Mellody,” Katie Harel, the restaurant’s managing director, told Forbes , “who were adamant that there would be something affordable in the café for everyone. So everyone can eat something in the café for $2. Every single person.” In addition to the grilled cheese option, the museum café also offers a $3 peanut butter and jelly sandwich.
Since no museum visit is complete without a trip to the gift shop, the Lucas Museum also offers some affordable souvenirs. The on-site shop sells 25¢ pencils listed as the Mellody Pencil . Part of the First Draft Collection , the stylish pencils include cheeky markings indicating how much of the pencil it would take to write a first, second, third, and final draft. The museum also offers a large selection of postcards for $2 each.
To plan your visit and book tickets, check out the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art website. To stay up to date with the museum, you can follow the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art on Instagram .

items.title: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
items.desc: Crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking weather, it's claimed.
items.text:
Some bin collections were missed partly because of the heatwave
Some bin collections were missed over the summer in a county partly because the heatwave became so serious it posed a risk to the lives of workers, a council worker has said.
Flintshire County Council's Chris Goddard said crews faced a "perfect storm" of challenges during the UK's record-breaking hot weather , causing a spate of widespread missed collections.
During the summer, drought was declared in all of Wales and wildfires caused devastation in parts of the country .
Goddard said: "We do have to make some difficult decisions but ultimately if there is a fatality in the workplace because of a decision I've made, that's something that I would have to live with - and probably defend."
Despite the missed collections the council remained on target to hit the Welsh government's national 70% waste recycling target this year, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.
Flintshire County Council is on track to hit its waste recycling target despite the disruption
Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.
"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.
"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.
"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."
Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.
"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.
"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."
Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.
The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.

items.title: Extreme weather leaves gardeners hedging their bets
items.desc: Gardeners across Sussex are changing their planting strategies after this year's unprecedented heat.
items.text:
Plants and trees from hotter parts of the world are being brought into Sussex
Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather.
West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought.
The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely.
Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there.
Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year.
"That's probably going to continue," he said.
"We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things.
"That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers."
This year's heat and lack of rainfall were unprecedented
Joe Whelan, head gardener at Nymans in Handcross, warned another year of drought could be "quite detrimental" on larger, more mature trees.
The gardeners said planting a greater diversity of species will be key to climate resilience, with plants from North America, southeastern Europe, central Asia, South Korea and Japan potentially faring better in future.
Chandler added it will not be a case of ripping out old plants and planting new species "in one go" but rather a gradual change over time with a "really diverse mix of things".
Whelan said it will be difficult to predict what will do well in the future.
It will be about "experimenting and accepting that some things probably aren't going to make it", he continued.

Unprecedented view of cosmos provided by Euclid mission throws up many more cases of gravitational lensing
A mission to create the largest ever 3D map of the universe has revealed more than 900m galaxies in its first major data release together with about 15,000 potential cases of a phenomenon that could help unlock the secrets of the “dark universe”.
Launched in July 2023, the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission promised to create the largest cosmic map ever made, encompassing a third of the sky and more than 10bn years of cosmic history.
The goal is to shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in the universe: the nature of dark energy and dark matter. These are thought to make up about 70% and 25% of the universe respectively.
Prof Andy Taylor, of the University of Edinburgh, who leads the UK science ground segment for the mission, said while there were bigger surveys, none had the detail and the information content of Euclid. By contrast the Hubble telescope has produced images of incredible resolution, but does not cover as large an area of the sky.
“The technological leap that’s Euclid is that we can keep that high resolution, but now we can basically map huge volumes of the sky, huge volumes of the universe,” Taylor said.
Now, the first major Euclid data release has landed, offering researchers an unprecedented view of the cosmos. “It’s the biggest high-resolution image of the universe we’ve ever had,” Taylor said.

“Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
One can only imagine the pause, double-take, or request for clarity which followed this comment, made by a woman’s elderly aunt in the midst of an effort to clean out her East Village apartment.
Yet as the woman, who revealed herself only as Betsy, rummaged around in that closet 4 years later, she found an oil painting of undulating hills, with soft earthen colors reminiscent of the female form, which is now known to be Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, painted by the Mother of Modernism in 1930.
Its rediscovery has been hailed as “a once-in-a-lifetime moment, and absolutely thrilling.”
Soon to be auctioned at Christie’s where it’s expected to garner around $3 million, the story of its provenance first broke at the New York Post , who talked to Betsy about the fateful closet-cleaning
Her aunt, she said, was an “extremely intelligent” former foreign service member who had received the painting from Georgia O’Keeffe’s Manhattan art dealer in 1963 as a graduation present from her parents. At the time time it cost $3,800.
Her aunt loved the painting, and hung it in the apartment for years. It ended up in the closet after she noticed that an evening during a bridge game, one of the players kept his eyes fixed on it for far too long.
“I think she was fully aware of its value … she recognized that it was an expression of her financial position,” Betsy told the Post.
She decided to take it down so as to not draw attention to herself during similar soirées. Amid her fur coats the painting sat, even after her niece came over in 2022 to help clean out the apartment as the woman prepared to enter hospice care. It was only after her aunt passed away that Betsy followed up on the comment of the “O’Keeffe in the closet” that she found it, still in its original box marked “The Downtown Gallery, 51st St.”

items.title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
items.desc: The decline has been put down to severe restrictions placed on the substances' use.
items.text:
Old landfill and industrial sites have been major sources of the chemicals in rivers like the Mersey
Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).
The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.
PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.
The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer. , external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last 10 years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in freshwater fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.
The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.
The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

items.desc: More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded at overflow sites previously unmonitored by Scottish Water, BBC Scotland News analysis has found.
items.text:
More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.
The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.
Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.
Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.
BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.
Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.
They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.
These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.
The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.
Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.
More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year – an average of about 274 a day.
It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.
The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.
